#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you can't exclude a transitive — except in uv*
The JVM has exclusions ([MS5](../../maven-demo/scenario-5-exclusions/guide.qmd)) and global bans ([MS18](../../maven-demo/scenario-18-banning/guide.qmd)). pip and Poetry have *neither* — and that gap is the scenario. `demo-lib-a` → `demo-lib-b` → `demo-lib-c`, and there is no pip or Poetry syntax for "install `demo-lib-a` but drop `demo-lib-c`". The most those two tools offer is to *override the version*. uv is the exception: it has a version override *and*, since 0.9.8, a real exclusion.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
Tested with **pip 25.3**, **Poetry 2.4**, **uv 0.11**. pip and Poetry have no transitive-exclusion mechanism at all. uv has `override-dependencies` (replaces a version graph-wide, 0.1+) and `exclude-dependencies` (removes a package from the graph, **0.9.8+**; scoped to a single edge from 0.11.25). Both are shown below.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Your project] --> LibA[demo-lib-a 1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[demo-lib-b 1.0.0]
    LibB -- "==1.0.0" --> LibC[demo-lib-c]
    Override[uv override] -. "forces 2.0.0" .-> LibC
    Exclude[uv exclusion] -. "removes" .-> LibC
```

pip / Poetry — no exclusion syntax exists; `demo-lib-c` is unavoidable:

```{.text include="pip/requirements.txt" snippet="p9-deps"}
```

uv, lever 1 — a version *override* (the package stays):

```{.toml include="uv/pyproject.toml" snippet="p9-uv-override"}
```

uv, lever 2 — an *exclusion* (the package goes):

```{.toml include="uv-exclude/pyproject.toml" snippet="p9-uv-exclude"}
```

#### ! Expect
Some equivalent of Maven's `<exclusion>` — a way to prune `demo-lib-c` from the graph.

#### ! Actual
In pip and Poetry there isn't one: `demo-lib-c` is installed no matter what, because you cannot tell either resolver to omit a package another package requires. uv's `override-dependencies` can *force* `demo-lib-c` to 2.0.0 against `demo-lib-b`'s `==1.0.0` pin, but it is still present. Only uv's `exclude-dependencies` actually removes it — `uv sync` installs `demo-lib-a` and `demo-lib-b` and nothing else, exactly as a Maven exclusion would.

#### ! Why
The JVM treats the classpath as something you assemble and can prune edge by edge. pip and Poetry treat the environment as the *closure* of what your dependencies declare they need — if `demo-lib-b` says it imports `demo-lib-c`, removing `demo-lib-c` would leave `demo-lib-b` broken at import time, so neither resolver will do it. Overrides exist because *version* disagreements are common and resolvable; exclusions mostly don't, because *removing* a declared need is, in that model, just breaking the package. uv takes the JVM's position instead: the declaration is advice, and the consumer may know better (the dependency is only used by an optional code path, say, or you ship a replacement). This is the mirror image of [MS18](../../maven-demo/scenario-18-banning/guide.qmd): where Maven can ban and Gradle/sbt can silently prune, pip and Poetry can only substitute — and uv can do both.

#### ! Fix
*   **You don't want a transitive's *version*:** override it — uv `override-dependencies`, or a constraints file ([P6](../scenario-6-constraints/guide.qmd)) to pin it to something acceptable.
*   **You don't want the transitive *at all*, and you use uv:** `exclude-dependencies`. Prefer the scoped form (`{ package = { name = "demo-lib-b" }, dependencies = ["demo-lib-c"] }`) so you cut one edge, not every path to the package.
*   **You don't want it at all, and you use pip or Poetry:** you can't, cleanly. The options are ugly: fork the intermediate package to drop the dependency, vendor it, or replace the whole dependency with one that doesn't pull the offender ([P11](../scenario-11-private-index/guide.qmd) covers private/patched packages).
*   **It's a security concern:** don't try to exclude — *audit and upgrade* ([P12](../scenario-12-audit/guide.qmd)). Pin the transitive to a fixed version via constraints.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Overriding a transitive's version to a compatible, tested release.
* MEDIUM Overriding to a version the intermediate package wasn't built against — you've recreated the diamond conflict ([P2](../scenario-2-conflict/guide.qmd)) by hand. Excluding a package the intermediate imports unconditionally — `ImportError` at the first call, exactly like an over-aggressive Maven exclusion.
* HIGH Forking or vendoring to "remove" a dependency, then carrying that patch forever with no upstream security updates.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:**

```bash
# pip / poetry: demo-lib-c is present and cannot be excluded
pip install -r requirements.txt && pip show demo-lib-c        # present, 1.0.0
poetry lock && grep 'name = "demo-lib-c"' poetry.lock         # present

# uv override (uv/): changes the VERSION but not the presence
uv sync && python -c "import demo_lib_c; print(demo_lib_c.__version__)"   # 2.0.0

# uv exclusion (uv-exclude/): the package is gone, its consumer is not
uv sync && uv pip list | grep demo-lib    # demo-lib-a, demo-lib-b — no demo-lib-c
```

**What to look for:** `demo-lib-c` present under pip and Poetry (1.0.0) and under the uv override (2.0.0); absent under the uv exclusion while `demo-lib-b` is still installed.

**Conclusion:** pip and Poetry can substitute a transitive's version but cannot remove it; uv can do either.

#### ! Takeaway
There is no `<exclusion>` in pip or Poetry. Overrides (uv) and constraints (pip) change *which version* of a required package you get; only uv's `exclude-dependencies` removes a package your dependencies declare they need. On the other two tools, the honest fixes live upstream.

#### ! Wild
This gap is a recurring source of frustration for teams moving from Maven to Python: "how do I just exclude the vulnerable transitive like I do in my POM?" For most of Python's history the answer was "you can't, you pin or upgrade it", which surprised people every time and is a large part of why Python security tooling leans so hard on *auditing* rather than *excluding*. uv added `exclude-dependencies` in 0.9.8 and a scoped form in 0.11.25, because users immediately discovered that an unscoped exclusion cuts every path to the package, not just the one they meant — the same lesson Maven users learn from [MS5](../../maven-demo/scenario-5-exclusions/guide.qmd).
